title: Numbers and age: six numbers that change their clothes
goal: Count from zero to millions, say your age, spell out a phone number, and recognize the six numbers that change shape to match the thing being counted.
bekal: numbers 1–10, the tens, hundreds and thousands
the six numbers that follow the noun class: *-moja, -wili, -tatu, -nne, -tano, -nane*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Wangapi nyumbani kwenu?
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon on the veranda, waiting for the rain to stop. Amina and Budi swap stories about their homes.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nina miaka ishirini na mitatu. Na wewe?
lines.literal: I-have years twenty and three. and you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: How many people are in your family?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Tuko watu saba: wazazi wawili na watoto watano.
lines.id: There are seven of us: two parents and five children.
lines.literal: we-are people seven: parents two and children five.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Watoto watano! Wewe ni wa ngapi?
lines.id: Five children! Which one are you?
lines.literal: children five! you are of how-many?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Mimi ni wa tatu. Kaka zangu wana miaka thelathini na ishirini na saba.
lines.id: I'm the third. My brothers are thirty and twenty-seven.
lines.literal: I am of three. brothers of-me they-have years thirty and twenty and seven.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Namba yako ya simu ni ngapi?
lines.literal: number of-you of phone is how-many?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Sifuri, saba, tano — mbili, tatu, nne — sita, saba, nane.
lines.id: Zero, seven, five — two, three, four — six, seven, eight.
lines.literal: zero, seven, five — two, three, four — six, seven, eight.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ngoja kidogo... sema tena polepole, tafadhali!
lines.id: Wait a moment... say it again slowly, please!
lines.literal: wait a-little... speak again slowly, please!

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Haya: sifuri, saba, tano... Unaandika sasa?
lines.id: Okay: zero, seven, five... Are you writing now?
lines.literal: okay: zero, seven, five... you-are-writing now?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Yes, I'm writing. Thank you very much, sis!

notes: **Age is measured with miaka, the plural of mwaka (year).** Literally "I have years twenty-three", exactly the way French and Spanish do it. The question is *Una miaka mingapi?* — and don't be surprised if people answer while asking you back; age is no secret in East Africa.
**Na means "and" and also joins numbers.** *Ishirini na tatu* = twenty and three = 23. *Mia moja hamsini na tano* = 155. All number joins use *na*, without exception.
**Tuko means "we are (located)".** This is the "be located" form that is set up fully in unit 8; for now just know that *tuko watu saba* is the most natural way to say "there are seven of us".
**Wa ngapi? asks for position, not quantity.** *Wewe ni wa ngapi?* = which child are you? The answer uses an ordinal: *wa kwanza* (first), *wa pili* (second), *wa tatu* (third).

**Ngoja means "wait" and haya means "okay".** Both are spoken-language words that rarely make it into textbooks but are heard a hundred times a day. *Haya basi* = "well, all right then", the most common way to close a conversation.

grammars.title: Numbers: the first ten, then everything else
body: The first ten numbers have to be memorized. After that Swahili counts in the most sensible way in the world: you just join them with *na*.
after: Notice the Arabic roots: *sifuri* (from *sifr*, zero — the same word that gave English "cipher" and "zero"), *ishirini* (Arabic *'ishrun*), *arobaini* (*arba'in*), *hamsini* (*khamsin*), *mia* (*mi'a*), *elfu* (*alf*). All the tens come from Arabic, while the units 1–10 are native Bantu.
Joining is always with *na*: **23** = *ishirini na tatu*, **47** = *arobaini na saba*, **99** = *tisini na tisa*, **156** = *mia moja hamsini na sita*, **2,024** = *elfu mbili na ishirini na nne*.
For money, people in Tanzania and Kenya say the thousands first: *elfu tano* (5,000), *elfu kumi* (10,000), *laki moja* (100,000 — a loan from Hindi *lakh*), *milioni moja* (1,000,000).

grammars.title: Six numbers that follow their noun class
body: Four numbers never change: **sita, saba, tisa, kumi** — and all the tens and hundreds. The remaining six have an empty prefix to be filled by the noun class: **-moja, -wili, -tatu, -nne, -tano, -nane**.
after: The *nyumba* class — the biggest class in Swahili, which you set up in unit 7 — happens to use the numbers in their bare form: *nyumba mbili*, *saa tatu*, *shilingi elfu tano*. That is why the forms *mbili*, *tatu*, *tano* are heard most often: they are the form of the class with the most members.
The number always comes **after** its noun: *watoto watano* (five children), not the reverse. Think of the English "children five" — the order is the opposite of English.

The question word *-ngapi* (how many) follows exactly the same rule: *watu wangapi?*, *vitabu vingapi?*, *miaka mingapi?*, *nyumba ngapi?*, *magari mangapi?*. If you're unsure of the form, just remember the number "two" for that noun — the prefix is the same.

sections.title: Wa kwanza, wa pili — ordinal numbers

blocks.text: Ordinal numbers are formed with the connector *-a* in front of the number. The form of that connector follows the noun class — *wa* for people, *cha* for *ki-* class things, *ya* for the *nyumba* class.

⚠️ Two surprises: "first" is not *wa moja* but **wa kwanza**, and "second" is not *wa mbili* but **wa pili**. After that the ordinary numbers are used. These two special words turn up everywhere: *daraja la kwanza* (first class), *mara ya pili* (the second time).
*Mara* means "time/occasion": *mara moja* (once — and also "immediately"), *mara mbili* (twice), *mara nyingi* (often), *mara ya kwanza* (for the first time).
Numbers rarely show up alone. The six rows below are where you'll hear them most.

head: Situation
Sentence
English
rows: My number is zero seven five...

blocks.text: Phone numbers are **always spelled digit by digit**, never grouped the way English speakers say "eight twenty-one". Zero is *sifuri*, and in casual talk it is often replaced by *ziro*.

For prices, people usually drop the word *shilingi* and just say the number: "*Elfu tatu*" is clear enough for three thousand shillings. What matters is that you catch the word *elfu* — that is where the zeros are.
